item.title: China says Japanese authorities fail to correct wrongdoings one year after erroneous remarks on Taiwan
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
China says Japanese authorities fail to correct wrongdoings one year after erroneous remarks on Taiwan BEIJING, Nov. 6 (Xinhua) -- The Japanese authorities have failed to show any sincerity or take action to reflect on and correct their wrongdoings one year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made erroneous comments on Taiwan at the Diet, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Friday. Guo made the remarks at a regular news briefing, stating that the current serious difficulties in China-Japan relations are entirely the responsibility of the Japanese side. It stems from the erroneous remarks made by the Japanese leader a year ago regarding Taiwan, which blatantly signaled a potential military intervention in the Taiwan question, challenged China's national sovereignty, and undermined the political foundation of China-Japan relations, Guo added. "Regrettably, one year on, the Japanese authorities have not moved at all. They've been evading the issue and yet to demonstrate any sincerity or take any action to reflect upon and correct the wrongdoings," he said. Noting that China's position on China-Japan relations has been consistent, he reiterated that for the Japanese side, the pressing priority is to correct the erroneous words and deeds on the Taiwan question, adopt a correct attitude on historical issues, and form an objective and rational perception on China.

item.title: Inflation in Taiwan exceeds warning threshold for 6th straight month
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-06
Inflation in Taiwan exceeds warning threshold for 6th straight month TAIPEI -- Consumer prices in the Taiwan region rose 2.33 percent in October from a year earlier, remaining above the island's inflation warning threshold for a sixth consecutive month, official data showed Thursday, as higher food, fuel and travel costs continued to put pressure on household budgets. The island's statistics agency said the consumer price index (CPI) edged up 0.06 percent from September. Core CPI, which excludes fresh vegetables, fruit and energy, increased 2.23 percent year on year. The agency mainly attributed October's inflation to higher prices for food, fuel and travel-related services. Food costs remained a particular burden for consumers, with egg prices climbing 11.45 percent year on year and the cost of edible oils rising 5.34 percent. Due to factors that included international oil prices, transportation costs on the island also increased. Housing-related expenses, including rents and residential management fees, are also on the rise. Meanwhile, inflationary pressures remained pronounced at the production level. Taiwan's producer price index (PPI) jumped nearly one-fifth in October from a year earlier, driven mainly by higher prices for petroleum and coal products, electronic products, and chemical materials. The PPI rose by an average of 11.12 percent in the first 10 months of the year, pointing to persistent cost pressures on producers that may be further passed on to consumers. Despite headline figures showing economic growth and rising per capita GDP, economists and commentators have pointed to deep-rooted structural problems in Taiwan's economy, including wage stagnation, soaring housing prices and overreliance on the semiconductor sector. Traditional industries and small businesses continue to face mounting pressure. Concerns over labor shortages, energy security and demographic decline have also weighed on the island's long-term economic outlook.

item.title: Satellite images of Taiwan highlight technological advancements and cross-Strait benefits
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
Satellite images of Taiwan highlight technological advancements and cross-Strait benefits High-resolution satellite images of Taiwan released by the mainland's Jilin-1 commercial satellite network showcase advances in aerospace technology and the potential of remote sensing services to benefit people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, a mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to widespread online attention to the recently released images, which offer detailed views of Taiwan's landscapes, including Sun Moon Lake and streets in Taipei. The images capture Taiwan's cities, farmland, salt fields, wetlands, and harbors, allowing people on both sides of the Strait to appreciate the island's natural beauty and prompting lively interactions on social media, Zhu said. She noted that the images not only demonstrate the mainland's technological progress but also highlight how people across the Strait can benefit from diverse remote sensing services and use technology to protect their shared home. Zhu expressed confidence that people on both sides would have more opportunities to appreciate the country's landscapes through different means in the future.

item.title: Mainland reaffirms Taiwan's ineligibility for Interpol membership
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
Mainland reaffirms Taiwan's ineligibility for Interpol membership Taiwan, as part of China, is not entitled to join the International Criminal Police Organization, a Chinese mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday, stressing that existing arrangements allow police authorities on the island to cooperate with their international counterparts. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities, which claimed that the island's exclusion from Interpol had created a gap in global security and called for international support for its membership. The 94th Interpol General Assembly is scheduled to take place in Hong Kong from Nov 30 to Dec 3. Zhu stated that the mainland's position on Taiwan's participation in international organizations has been consistent and clear: such matters must be handled in accordance with the one-China principle. She said China and Interpol have made appropriate arrangements for Taiwan's participation in cooperation and activities under the organization's framework, with functioning channels for information sharing and case cooperation between Taiwan's police authorities and Interpol member states' central bureaus worldwide. Zhu criticized the DPP authorities for repeatedly politicizing Taiwan's participation in international organizations, saying their attempts to pursue separatism were doomed to fail. Separately, responding to a question about Taiwan's participation in this year's APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, Zhu said the mainland has consistently handled the matter in accordance with the one-China principle, relevant APEC memorandums of understanding, and established practices. Taiwan can participate as long as these arrangements are followed, she said.

item.title: Mainland spokeswoman denies DPP allegations of election interference
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
Mainland spokeswoman denies DPP allegations of election interference A Chinese mainland spokeswoman on Wednesday rejected allegations by Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities that the mainland was attempting to interfere in the island's local elections, calling the claims groundless and a distortion of facts. Zhu Fenglian, spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to statements by Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te and the DPP authorities warning of alleged mainland "cognitive warfare" and election interference through criminal gangs or local collaborators. Zhu accused the DPP authorities of repeatedly manipulating anti-mainland sentiment, particularly during election periods, by spreading false allegations of mainland interference. She said such tactics were intended to divert attention from the DPP authorities' poor governance, stir up hostility toward the mainland, and win votes. An increasing number of Taiwan residents were seeing through these political maneuvers, she added.

item.title: Taiwan has no right to join Interpol: mainland spokeswoman
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
Taiwan has no right to join Interpol: mainland spokeswoman BEIJING -- Taiwan, as part of China, does not have the right to become an Interpol member, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office said on Wednesday. Spokeswoman Zhu Fenglian made the remarks at a regular news conference in response to a media query about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities' call for international support for Taiwan's inclusion in Interpol, from which the island has been excluded for decades. Interpol, an intergovernmental organization for police cooperation in combating crime, has 196 member countries, each hosting a National Central Bureau"The participation of the Taiwan region in activities of international organizations must be in accordance with the one-China principle. This has been our consistent and clear position," Zhu said. The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC. The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. Zhu noted that China and Interpol have already made proper arrangements for the Taiwan region to participate in cooperation and activities under the Interpol framework. Police authorities in the Taiwan region have unimpeded channels for information sharing and cooperation on cases with Interpol National Central Bureaus in all member countries, she added. The DPP authorities have been trying to deceive people on the island through repeated political manipulation over Taiwan's participation in international organizations, but their attempts to seek "Taiwan independence" via provocations will inevitably fail, the spokeswoman said.

item.title: Mainland to further ease travel for Taiwan residents
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
Mainland to further ease travel for Taiwan residents The Chinese mainland will continue to facilitate travel and exchanges across the Taiwan Strait, a mainland spokesperson said on Wednesday, citing growing passenger traffic, rising tourism interest and measures to make visits more convenient for Taiwan residents. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a regular news conference, where she also rejected allegations by Taiwan's "mainland affairs council" regarding the safety of Taiwan residents visiting the mainland. The "mainland affairs council" recently claimed that an increasing number of Taiwan residents had gone missing or been detained for questioning on the mainland, saying it would maintain its orange travel alert — the second-highest level — for the mainland, Hong Kong and Macao. The Democratic Progressive Party authorities have fabricated so-called missing-person data, concocted false information and spread rumors to smear the mainland, intimidate Taiwan compatriots, and disrupt and undermine normal cross-Strait exchanges and interactions, Zhu said. She said the mainland is among the safest places in the world, adding that Taiwan residents who work, live and travel there have experienced its safety and quality of life firsthand. The remarks came amid growing interest in individual travel to the mainland reported at a recent tourism fair in Taichung. Zhu said the mainland has introduced a series of measures to make travel more convenient for Taiwan residents. These include waiving travel permit application fees for first-time visitors, allowing single-entry travel permits to be issued at 100 ports of entry, and offering free or discounted admission to most A-rated tourist attractions for first-time visitors. She also noted growing interest among Taiwan travelers in cultural tourism, with more visitors exploring museums and exhibitions to gain a deeper understanding of Chinese history and culture. Cross-Strait passenger traffic has continued to increase. According to the Gaoqi border inspection station in Xiamen, Fujian province, the Xiamen-Kinmen ferry routes handled more than 1.74 million passenger trips as of Oct 26, including nearly 1.4 million trips by Taiwan residents, accounting for about 80 percent of the total. Both figures have already surpassed their full-year totals for 2025, setting new annual records since services resumed in 2023. More than 70,000 Taiwan residents entered the mainland through the routes for the first time this year, an increase of more than 70 percent year-on-year. Zhu said the approximately 30-minute ferry journey, with 24 scheduled services daily, has made same-day travel between Xiamen and Kinmen convenient. Travel purposes have also expanded beyond family visits to include business, education, cultural exchanges and tourism. Separately, Zhu welcomed a recent incident in Shanghai in which traffic police recovered and returned a handbag lost by a member of a Taiwan actor's team. She described the incident as heartwarming and encouraged more Taiwan residents, particularly young people, to visit the mainland and experience its development firsthand. On economic exchanges, Zhu said the mainland would continue helping Taiwan farmers and fishermen expand their sales in its vast market. Imports of fishery products from Taiwan rose 35.5 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters, according to figures previously released by the Taiwan Affairs Office. Zhu said the mainland would continue implementing the 10 measures introduced in April this year to promote cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation, including support for Taiwan's agricultural and fishery products entering the mainland market. She criticized the DPP authorities for placing obstacles in the way of agricultural cooperation, saying the mainland would continue helping Taiwan producers reach more consumers and share the benefits of cross-Strait economic integration.

item.title: One-China principle emphasized
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
One-China principle emphasized Cross-Strait representatives gathered on Sunday to mark the 81st anniversary of Taiwan's restoration to the motherland, stressing that both sides belong to one China and expressing firm opposition to "Taiwan independence" separatism and external interference. A symposium in Fu-zhou, Fujian province, brought together around 200 attendees, including descendants of revolutionary martyrs who sacrificed their lives in Taiwan and Taiwan compatriots who resisted Japanese aggression, cross-Strait youth, experts, scholars and representatives from the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions and overseas. The event came one year after a decision by the national legislature to designate Oct 25 as the Commemoration Day of Taiwan's Restoration, the day in 1945 when Taiwan was officially returned to China after half a century of Japanese colonial occupation. Song Tao, head of the Taiwan Work Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said that the establishment of the commemorative day demonstrated the country's firm confidence in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and solidified the international community's adherence to the one-China principle. Song emphasized that compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Strait must jointly carry forward the great spirit of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45), while firmly opposing "Taiwan independence" separatism and external interference. It is essential to promote Chinese culture to strengthen national pride and boost the confidence of the Chinese people, he said, adding that the Chinese mainland will firmly support the patriotic reunification forces within the island and steadfastly advance national reunification. Hung Hsiu-chu, former chairwoman of the Chinese Kuomintang party, recalled the crimes committed by the Japanese aggressors against Chinese people and warned that people must remain strictly vigilant against Japan's attempts to revive militarism. Hung criticized Taiwan's current Democratic Progressive Party authorities for attempting to erase the history of the war against Japanese invasion and Taiwan's restoration from the school curriculum, which she said left younger generations unaware of their roots and created a confused identity that remained a fundamental cause of Taiwan's internal rift and cross-Strait tensions. Ou Kuei-chih, a retired Chinese literature teacher from Taipei First Girls' High School, said that only by learning history can young people discover their roots, understand the past suffering of the nation, and find answers on how to avoid the danger of war caused by cross-Strait division. Encouraging Taiwan youths to visit the mainland for more exchanges, she said students must break through the bias of the island's media to search for the truth, explore why textbooks differ, and make their own rational judgments. Chiu Chih-shien, secretary-general of the Taiwan Restoration Commemoration Association, said that Taiwan's restoration was a core achievement of the war against Japanese aggression, noting that this historic day was once widely celebrated through various public activities before the DPP's deliberate erasure led to its gradual fading from public memory over the past decades. Chiu said that the legislation last year had prompted many Taiwan compatriots to reflect on why local textbooks and media in Taiwan remained silent while the mainland highly valued the anniversary, inspiring people to recognize its true historical value. He added that civic groups on the island should work together to hold more public activities so that people can learn the real history and understand how restoration benefits them.

item.title: Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Chinese mainland spokesperson slams Lai Ching-te's flattering remarks on Japan Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-02-11
BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday denounced Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te for ignoring the heinous crimes committed by Japan during its colonial rule over Taiwan, describing their flattering remarks toward Japan as utterly disgraceful. Zhu Fenglian, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to a media inquiry about Lai's intention to work with Japan to "deal with regional challenges." Zhu also urged the Japanese side to retract Sanae Takaichi's erroneous remarks on Taiwan, handle Taiwan-related issues prudently, and abide by the one-China principle with concrete actions. item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for imposing restrictions and obstacles on cross-Strait exchanges in pursuit of their "Taiwan independence" agenda and selfish gains. The DPP authorities, led by Lai Ching-te, are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait interactions and their acts have drawn strong criticism from various sectors in Taiwan, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday. Zhu expressed the hope that Taiwan compatriots will firmly oppose the retrogressive actions of the DPP authorities and promote exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait in various fields. She noted that cross-Strait flight routes have been disrupted due to interference from the DPP authorities, with previously operated destinations yet to resume normal operations. In 2025, the average passenger load factor on cross-Strait routes reached 80 percent, reflecting the strong need for direct flights between the two sides of the Strait, Zhu said. "We hope that the Taiwan side will heed public opinion and lift unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transport as soon as possible," she added.
